analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements requiring workers to pay union fees as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: Backed by 32 Republican senators, the bill sat on the Senate calendar for nearly two years and never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change two federal labor laws so that no employer and union anywhere in the country could agree that workers must join a union or pay union fees to keep their job. Today, at least 27 states already ban these agreements on their own; this bill would extend that rule to every state, including the roughly 20 states where unions and employers can still negotiate them. The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 2023 and never moved after being placed on the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, employees at unionized workplaces who did not want to support the union would keep their full share of union-negotiated wages and benefits without paying any fees. Employers would also gain: unions would collect less money and have less bargaining leverage, which makes it harder for them to negotiate pay, staffing, and safety terms and to organize new workplaces. CRS notes at least 27 states already have such laws; this would make it national.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that let an employer and union agree to require union membership as a condition of employment.
It would apply to every agreement entered into or renewed after enactment, extending rules that CRS says at least 27 states have already adopted to the whole country.

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose the dues and fees that come from requiring all workers they represent to contribute, leaving them with less money to bargain, enforce contracts, and organize. Union members and the workers unions represent would bear the indirect cost: weaker union finances generally mean weaker bargaining results on wages and working conditions, while unions would still be legally required to represent every worker in the bargaining unit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and the workers they represent

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the requirement that workers covered by a union contract pay for the cost of their own representation, so employees could take union-negotiated wages and benefits without contributing anything to the union that negotiated them.

Unions would collect less money nationwide, and they would still be legally obligated to represent all workers in a bargaining unit, so the same duty would be funded by fewer people — the classic free-rider problem this kind of law creates.

The bill also strikes the union-security provision of the Railway Labor Act, ending these agreements for airline and railroad workers, groups whose bargaining has historically been among the most heavily unionized.
Supporters would have to concede that unions lose dues income immediately and that workplaces where unions rely on security agreements would become harder to sustain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefit is individual: no worker would have to pay union fees to keep a job. But the cost is broad and structural. Unions must represent every worker in a bargaining unit whether or not that worker pays, so stripping the payment requirement defunds representation. The realistic result is weaker unions, fewer resources for negotiating and enforcing contracts, and lower wage growth in the roughly 20 states that do not already have such laws. The bill offers no replacement mechanism for funding the representation it requires unions to keep providing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever took it up and no senator ever voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on February 27, 2023, joined by 21 original Senate cosponsors named in the bill text.
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on February 28, 2023 — the routine early step after introduction, not committee consideration.
All 31 cosponsors who joined were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

No committee hearings, markups, or floor votes appear in the action history; the bill's last recorded action was the February 28, 2023 placement on the calendar, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
At least 27 states already prohibit these agreements under their own laws, so the bill's practical effect would have been limited to the remaining states.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the unionized workers who depend on union security agreements for funding are better off because the bill died — their existing agreements stay intact. The status quo also left employers in right-to-work states no worse off, since most states already had such laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Labor unions kept their funding rules

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on February 27, 2023.

for.name: 31 Republican senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Barrasso, Cruz, Cornyn, Grassley, Scott (SC), Scott (FL), and Lee
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors; the 21 original cosponsors were named when the bill was introduced and the roster grew to 31, all Republicans.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate floor and committee schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote and took no action to advance it; the bill's last recorded action was its placement on the Senate calendar in February 2023.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Republicans, and no vote was ever taken, so the fight never produced a roll-call — but on paper the divide was fully partisan.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the agreements that let unions require the workers they represent to pay fees, cutting union dues income nationwide and leaving unions with the same duty to represent all workers but fewer contributors. Union finances and worker bargaining power rise and fall together, so the union interest and the interest of unionized workers largely run together here.

industries.industry: Employers in heavily unionized sectors (airlines, railroads, autos, manufacturing)
industries.note: Weaker union funding and no union-security agreements mean less organized pressure on wages, benefits, and staffing. Employers gain negotiating leverage that comes at the expense of the workers on the other side of the table.
